What's Going Up at Cayuga: Duke's New Gas Plant in Vermillion County, Explained

Two big turbines, a court case and a 2030 finish line. Here's the public record, in plain English.

Sol R. Panel

Drive north from our shop in Clinton and you'll pass one of the biggest construction jobs in the Wabash Valley. On May 14, 2026, Duke Energy ceremonially broke ground on the Cayuga Energy Complex, two new natural gas units at the Cayuga Generating Station here in Vermillion County. Crews had already started grading the site and laying underground piping.

If you've wondered what's going on up there, here's what the public record says as of late July 2026, and what it does and doesn't mean for your own power.

What's Being Built at Cayuga

The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved the project on October 29, 2025, in Cause No. 46193. The order covers two combined-cycle natural gas units, each rated at about 738 megawatts in winter, for roughly 1,476 megawatts combined. Combined cycle means the plant captures heat from the gas turbines' exhaust to make steam for a second set of turbines, squeezing more electricity out of the same fuel.

A few numbers from the record:

  • Cost: the IURC approved an estimated construction cost of about $3.32 billion, plus financing costs during construction.
  • Timeline: Duke testified it plans to put the first unit in service by September 1, 2029 and the second by May 29, 2030.
  • Capacity: Duke says the new units will raise Cayuga's generating capacity by 470 megawatts, to 1,476 megawatts in total.
  • Age of the old plant: Duke calls Cayuga the oldest coal-fired power plant on its Indiana system, with nearly six decades of service.

Duke Energy Indiana, which serves about 930,000 customers, argued the plant is needed as the state grows. WFYI reported that the IURC found the proposal satisfied Indiana's five pillars of energy policy: reliability, resilience, stability, affordability and environmental sustainability.

The Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, the state's ratepayer advocate, recommended denying the request as proposed. The IURC held public field hearings on the case in Bloomington and Terre Haute on April 17, 2025.

What Happens to the Coal Units

This part changed along the way. Duke's original plan pointed toward retiring the Cayuga coal units. Then, as WFYI reported, a June 2025 settlement with the coal trade group Reliable Energy, Inc. led Duke to study whether the existing coal units could stay online and be sold to a third party. Duke's May 2026 groundbreaking release says that feasibility study is underway. As of late July 2026, no sale had been announced in those sources.

The Court Fight Over How It's Paid For

The IURC also approved "construction work in progress" ratemaking for the project. WFYI explained that this lets Duke charge customers for the project while the plant is being built, which reduces the utility's financing costs. Duke said the approach will save customers money over the life of the plant. Citizens Action Coalition and Vote Solar disagreed and appealed.

On April 16, 2026, the Indiana Supreme Court took the appeal directly from the Court of Appeals at Duke's request. The order set briefing deadlines running through August 21, 2026, and scheduled oral argument for September 17, 2026. The appeal does not stop proceedings at the IURC. As of this writing, there's no ruling.

What It Means for Your Own Power

Here's the practical takeaway for a homeowner or farmer in Vermillion, Parke or Vigo County. Decisions about Cayuga are made by Duke, the IURC and the courts, on a timeline that runs to 2030. You don't get a vote on the turbines.

You do get a say in what happens at your own meter. A solar array on your roof, or a ground mount out by the pole barn, makes power right where you use it. Pair it with LiFePO4 battery storage or a Kohler standby generator and you've got your own backup plan, whatever the grid is doing. Accutek Solar has been pulling wire in this county since 1994, and that kind of local, right-sized power is what we build.

None of that is a knock on the folks building Cayuga. The new plant is a big deal for Vermillion County, and Duke says the project will support more than 3,700 jobs. It's simply a reminder that the biggest decisions about the grid get made far from your kitchen table. The ones about your own home don't have to be.
